editorNote: This week’s Atari dispatch joins the games, software and equipment in the May computer magazines.
morningLine: Ten-dollar games crowd the rack as Atari prepares its return to the show floor.

lead.headline: Mastertronic pitches Commodore games at $9.99
lead.dek: A $9.99 price tag brings a fresh budget pitch to the Commodore 64 shelf.
body: Mastertronic is making price the attraction on the Commodore 64 games rack. The May issue of COMPUTE! reports games at $9.99 apiece, a modest entry ticket for owners looking beyond the familiar full-price boxes. This is the month’s product-news coverage, not a claim that the games all arrived during this particular week.

The advertised selection ranges from Chiller and BMX Racer to Dark Star, Magic Carpet and More Adventures of Big Mac. The notice also names Monty Python’s Quest for the Holy Grail. Its stated total and printed list do not line up neatly, but the consumer proposition is plain: individual C64 games for less than ten dollars.

For players who would rather build than buy another fixed challenge, the company announces The Games Creator for the C64 at $19.99. Scrolling scenery, sound effects and animated multicolored sprites are among the promised tools, with no programming required according to the vendor. That promise is not a hands-on verdict.

VIC-20 owners are included in the plans, with tape versions of games expected and a forthcoming construction package called The Games Designer priced at $12.99. Expected products should stay on the watch list until they reach the counter; the low-price campaign is news enough without turning a forecast into a delivery receipt.

stories.headline: Atari rejoins Summer CES; ST clears FCC hurdle
body: Atari is returning to the Summer Consumer Electronics Show after reversing its April decision to withdraw. The Los Angeles Times reports the change on May 17, following speculation that the earlier withdrawal signaled difficulties bringing the new ST computer to market.

Sigmund Hartmann, president of Atari’s software division, says the machine has cleared FCC requirements for United States sales. He also says shipments to Europe are under way and predicts American shipping will begin in July. Those are Atari’s statements and timetable, not independently established retail availability.

The report supplies no confirmed shop price or specific retail configuration. For prospective buyers, the immediate news is the regulatory hurdle and renewed show participation; final packages and deliveries remain the questions to watch.

stories.headline: GEM brings the desktop metaphor to PCs and Atari
body: Digital Research’s GEM offers icons, pull-down menus, movable overlapping windows and folders to computer owners accustomed to command lines. Selby Bateman’s May COMPUTE! feature describes Graphics Environment Manager as an interface layer, not a replacement operating system.

The attraction extends to developers. Digital Research’s Thomas Byers says application source can be reused and recompiled for Atari machines. That is a development bridge between processors, not a promise that IBM PC programs can simply be loaded as identical binaries on an ST.

The $500 developer toolkit includes Desktop, drivers, documentation, sample applications, a symbolic debugger and a Resource Construction Set. Planned applications include GEM Draw, GEM Wordchart and GEM Presentation Master, while Lifetree is adapting Volkswriter as Gem Write. Broad software support remains a task to accomplish, not an automatic benefit of a mouse.

stories.headline: Star offers near-letter-quality printing from $299
body: Star Micronics puts a $299 price on the SG-10 in the May COMPUTE! product notices. The ten-inch dot-matrix model is rated at 120 characters per second in draft mode and 30 in near-letter-quality printing. The slower second figure is the tradeoff behind the more finished page.

The SG, SD and SR families combine Star’s standard and PC lines through switch selection, with ten- and fifteen-inch carriage choices. The $799 SR-15 carries a 200-cps rating; that must not be read as its near-letter-quality speed.

Other listed alternatives include the $199 STX-10 thermal printer and $499 Powertype daisywheel. These are published product specifications and prices rather than an independent speed test, so a buyer still needs to check the computer connection and intended workload.

storeShelves.label: Top 5 Computer Games — editorial selections, not sales rankings
items: Rescue Raiders — Sir-Tech’s Apple disk game is listed at $34.95. The May COMPUTE! vendor notice describes a helicopter defending a European city, resource efficiency and strategy scoring, and eight battles followed by historical city notes. Do not call May 13 its launch date.

Ghostbusters — Antic May review by Harvey Bernstein lists Atari 48K disk at $29.95. Franchise economics and equipment purchases frame ghost-catching action; reviewer likes play but criticizes manually recorded account numbers and endlessly repeating music. A review of an existing game, not a new May release.

Spy vs. Spy — Antic May review by Harvey Bernstein lists Atari 48K disk at $29.95, First Star Software. Two-player or computer opposition, traps, five objects and split-screen Simulvision; the review strongly recommends it.
Beyond Castle Wolfenstein — Antic May review lists Muse Software’s Atari 32K disk at $34.95. Harvey Bernstein notes synthesized German speech but criticizes repetitive strategy and loading time.
Chiller — Mastertronic C64 budget selection in the May COMPUTE! product notice; $9.99, not a verified exact-week launch.

market.headline: Budget games meet a developing desktop market
market.summary: Mastertronic competes at $9.99 per C64 game while Digital Research courts software builders with a $500 GEM toolkit. These May published prices describe different bets on the home-computer market, not sales totals.

worldAnchor.headline: Antarctic spring ozone losses challenge prevailing models
worldAnchor.summary: In the May 16 print issue of Nature, British Antarctic Survey researchers Farman, Gardiner and Shanklin report large springtime Antarctic ozone losses and examine chlorine-related chemistry. The journal’s online publication metadata says May 1; May 16 is the dated print issue.

bbsNote.headline: File transfers and the 2400-bps buying dilemma
bbsNote.summary: May 1985 telecomputing coverage explains how beginners can move files and why faster modems are not automatically the best value. These are editorial summaries of period columns, not invented BBS messages.

posts.text: Arlan R. Levitan’s May column describes compatible terminal software, text capture and error checking, and identifies XMODEM on BBSs, CompuServe and Delphi.

posts.platform: Creative Computing / The Source and CompuServe
posts.text: Russ Lockwood’s May buyer’s guide discusses 300, 1200 and 2400-bps modems. It argues 300 bps can suffice for chat on The Source and games on CompuServe, while file transfers benefit from higher speed. It warns of speed surcharges and limited 2400-bps support.

Lockwood names Hayes, US Robotics, Racal-Vadic and other 2400-bps suppliers and discusses V.22bis. He estimates external modems can cost about $100 more than internal ones, but notes portability between computers. This is a general differential, not a verified specific-model price.

curiosity.headline: Portable color, with a 35-pound workout
curiosity.summary: The ISM Express brings an RGB monitor along for the trip, at a considerable weight.
curiosity.detail: Russ Lockwood’s May Creative Computing review weighs the PC-compatible at 35 pounds and complains that its carrying strap needs thicker padding. Base dual-floppy model: $3,195. The evaluation unit had a Panasonic monitor; the manufacturer was switching production to Sony, so do not describe the reviewer’s screen as Sony.
